briefs.headline: Szmyt's 56-yard kick lifts Browns past Steelers 27-24
briefs.summary: Andre Szmyt's career-long field goal with 10 seconds left Thursday night put Cleveland at 3-1 for the first time since 2001 after Pittsburgh erased a 14-point deficit to tie it. Deshaun Watson threw for 268 yards.

briefs.headline: Bengals hold Dugger, Hill and Risner out of practice again

coming_in.item: Tomorrow. The migratory bird summary, downloaded from wvdnr.gov again this morning with certificate verification on, HTTP 200, and read as text, opens the regular duck season Saturday, Oct. 3, for a first segment through Oct. 11, then Nov. 7-15 and Dec. 21-Jan. 31. The daily bag is six ducks and the possession limit 18, in aggregate, with no more than four mallards (two of them hens), two black ducks, three pintails, three wood ducks, two redheads, two canvasbacks and four sea ducks (no more than three scoters and three long-tailed ducks); scaup carry their own line inside the six, one a day Oct. 3-11, Nov. 7-15 and Dec. 21-Jan. 11, and two a day Jan. 12-31. Coots run the same dates at 15 and 45, mergansers at five and 15 in aggregate, and gallinules Oct. 3-11 and Dec. 2-Jan. 31 at 15 and 45. The second youth waterfowl day is Oct. 31, and footnote b lets youth hunters take two scaup inside the six-duck bag. HIP registration is required. Hunting hours for waterfowl in the controlled area at McClintic WMA end at noon Oct. 3-11 and concurrent hunting is prohibited there that week. The first segment closes Sunday, Oct. 11, so it opens and closes inside the two-week window.
coming_in.publication: West Virginia Migratory Bird Hunting Regulations Summary, September 2026 - January 2027

coming_in.species: Canada, white-fronted, snow and blue geese
coming_in.item: Tomorrow. The regular Canada and white-fronted goose season opens Saturday, Oct. 3, through Oct. 18, then Nov. 7-15 and Dec. 8-Jan. 31, five a day and 15 in possession in aggregate; snow and blue geese carry identical dates and limits on the table read this morning, and brant is Jan. 2-31 at one and three. The early Canada goose season closed Sept. 13. Tundra and trumpeter swans, king and clapper rails, eiders, whistling ducks, mottled ducks and harlequin ducks are listed as closed seasons. HIP registration is required.
coming_in.publication: West Virginia Migratory Bird Hunting Regulations Summary, September 2026 - January 2027

coming_in.item: Tomorrow. The third gun window for bear runs Saturday, Oct. 3, through Friday, Oct. 9, in SELECTED COUNTIES, so it opens and closes inside the two-week window. The summary table does not carry the county list, so no county is named here; the counties, rules and limits are on pamphlet pages 33-39 and vary by permit class, and the table's own line reads one a day, two in possession and two for the season while its limits note sends the reader to those pages, so no limit is printed here as settled. Electronic registration is required. Later windows are Oct. 22-25, Nov. 23-Dec. 6 and Dec. 7-31, all under the same selected-counties flag.

HIP registration is required for all three. The falconry limit on the table's footnote a is three migratory game birds a day and nine in possession, in aggregate.

prime.item: The Marine Fisheries recreational limits page, opened this morning at HTTP 200 and dated effective Sept. 2, 2026, prints red drum at 18 inches minimum and 27 inches maximum total length, one a day; its footnote C makes any red drum over 27 inches unlawful to possess and bars gigging, spearing or gaffing them, and the flounder proclamation's general information notes that red drum harvest must be reported to the division. On today's Hampstead tides the drum window is the last of the ebb, about 6:30 to the 8:31 p.m. low, in the dark; the Fisherman's Post October report, posted Thursday and one day old, has red drum as the main inshore target, slot fish with over-slots mixed in from the surf and piers, and reds schooled in the bays at 22 to 28 inches and better.

Limits page: 14 to 20 inches total length, three a day, with one of the three allowed over 26 inches. First light, which lands near the 7:18 a.m. low and the start of the flood, and the dock lights on the night flood after the 8:31 p.m. low are the windows on today's tide, with the water at Beaufort, 60 miles up the coast, at 78.4 degrees at 5:36 a.m., up 1.4 from Thursday's 77.0. The Oct. 1 shop reports, one day old, have the trout not yet ready, a few on topwater in the first hour of light and then live shrimp under slip corks in 15 to 20 feet, and say that will change as the water cools.

prime.species: Spanish mackerel, bluefish and king mackerel
prime.item: Limits page: Spanish mackerel 12-inch fork length, 15 a day; king mackerel 24-inch fork length, three a day, both carrying footnote H, which points to the South Atlantic council and the most recent mackerel proclamation for seasons; bluefish no minimum, 5/Day on the table, with footnote M setting five a day for private anglers and seven on a for-hire vessel. The surf at Ocean City Beach pier floods from the 5:37 a.m. low to the 12:26 p.m. high, the calm-morning, birds-over-bait window the reference describes for Spanish and blues on Gotcha plugs and metal jigs. The Oct. 1 Fisherman's Post report has Spanish plentiful and getting bigger from the surf and piers, 14 to 22 inches outside the inlet in 15 to 20 feet of water, kings to 32 pounds off Jolly Roger Pier, and the nearshore king bite still slow by the inshore shops' account.

Limits page: black drum 14 inches minimum and 25 inches maximum total length, 10 a day, with footnote C allowing one over 25 inches; sheepshead 14 inches total length, five a day. Both fish want moving water against structure, so the bridge pilings and oyster rocks on the ebb from the 1:41 p.m. high toward 8:31 p.m., or the flood after it, not the slack. The Oct. 1 Fisherman's Post report, one day old, has black drum of 3 to 4 pounds on shrimp at the bridges and oyster reefs and black drum in the evening bottom-fishing bags at Jolly Roger and Surf City piers, with sheepshead in Seaview Pier's mixed bag.

going_out.method: First segment of a three-way split

The dove first segment, open since Sept. 1, closes Sunday, Oct. 11, on the migratory bird table read this morning; the second segment opens Nov. 2, outside two weeks, and the third Dec. 7-Jan. 10. The limit is 15 a day and 45 in possession, shooting hours are noon to sunset on opening day and a half hour before sunrise to sunset after that, and HIP registration is required. The ducks, scaup and gallinule first segments that open tomorrow also close Oct. 11.

sections.label: On the Water

waters.reading: 103.0 cfs, 1.65 feet at 5:15 a.m., flagged falling against 159.0 cfs and 1.92 feet in the fetcher's comparison.
waters.working: The recession in its eighth day and still going, a little faster than Thursday. The USGS two-day trace, pulled at 5:48 a.m., has the river stepping down without a pause: 128 cfs and 1.78 feet at 5:15 a.m. Thursday, the true 24-hour mark and Thursday's edition reading, 126 at 6:15 and 7:15, 124 at 8:15, 122 from 9:15 a.m. through 1:15 p.m., 120 at 2:15 and 3:15, 118 at 4:15 through 6:15 p.m., 116 at 7:15, 114 at 8:15 and 9:15, 112 at 10:15 and 11:15, 110 at 12:15 a.m., 108 at 1:15, 106 at 2:15 and 3:15, 105 at 4:15 and 103 at 5:15, the window's low. That is down 25 cfs and 0.13 feet on the day, about 1 cfs an hour, and down 2 cfs over the last hour, so the fetcher's falling flag is right on the day and right at the hour; its 159 cfs and 1.92 feet are the first point of its own two-day window, 6 a.m. Wednesday, not 24 hours ago, and happen to be Wednesday's edition reading. The read string is the fetcher's flow-band verdict, prime wading water for the fourth morning, and this is the lowest the gauge has read since the flush: the pocket water is crossable at every tailout, the plunge pools fish from the head, and the undercut banks can be worked from the inside. No water temperature came back from the gauge. At 103 and clear, eight days after the flush, this is the long-leader, small-fly problem in full: a 12-foot leader to 6X and a size 18 caddis or a size 16 to 18 stonefly dry on the pocket seams and along the undercut banks in the low morning light, a size 18 caddis pupa on an unweighted dropper through the plunge-pool tailouts, and a sculpin pattern swung tight to the undercuts at dusk when the bigger fish come to the banks; with 25 cfs less than Thursday the tailouts are thin enough that the fish are in the pool heads and under the banks, so the approach is from below, the first cast at each pool is the one that counts, and wading in the pool itself is the surest way to end it.
waters.note: The fetcher's 159.0 cfs and 1.92 feet comparison point is the first point of its two-day window, 6 a.m. Wednesday, not 24 hours ago, and matches the trace's first point exactly (and is Wednesday's edition reading); the trace's true 24-hour mark is 128 cfs and 1.78 feet at 5:15 a.m. Thursday, which is Thursday's edition reading, so the falling flag is right on the day, down 25 cfs and 0.13 feet, and right at the hour, down 2 cfs from 105 at 4:15 to 103 at 5:15 a.m. The fetcher's numbers, flag and read string are printed as written; the Thursday recession and the overnight figures are the trace's, pulled at 5:48 a.m. No water temperature came back from the gauge. The Weather Service's active list for West Virginia at 5:46 a.m. returned zero products, so nothing is active on Webster County. The wvdnr.gov trout-stocking page was not opened this morning and nothing is printed on stocking.

waters.near: 14 miles above R.C. Byrd Locks and Dam
waters.reading: 24.65 feet at 5 a.m., flagged steady against 24.78 in the fetcher's comparison.
waters.read: 24.6 ft — normal pool. Ordinary bank access.
waters.working: At normal pool and down a half foot on the day, which the fetcher's steady flag does not show: 25.16 at 5 a.m. Thursday, the true 24-hour mark and Thursday's edition reading, against 24.65 this morning, down 0.51. The trace between them is a morning drop and then the usual pool sawtooth: 25.04 at 6 a.m. Thursday, 24.97 at 7, 24.88 at 8, 24.72 at 9, 24.70 at 10, 24.59 at 11 and noon, 24.70 at 1 p.m., 24.69 at 2, 24.67 at 3, 24.64 at 4, 24.57 at 5, 24.58 at 6, 24.55 at 7, 24.61 at 8, 24.71 at 9, 24.73 at 10, 24.76 at 11 p.m., 24.73 at midnight, 24.72 at 1 a.m., 24.67 at 2, 24.66 at 3 and 4, and 24.65 at 5 a.m. So the fetcher's steady flag is wrong on the day, a half-foot fall being outside anything it would call steady, and right at the hour, where the pool is down 0.01 in the last hour and has moved a tenth in six hours; the window's crest was 25.26 at 3 a.m. Thursday and its trough 24.54 Thursday evening. The fetcher's 24.78 is the first point of its own two-day window, about 5:45 a.m. Wednesday, not 24 hours ago; the trace pulled at 5:48 starts at 6 a.m. Wednesday and reads 24.93 there. The read string is the fetcher's band verdict, normal pool, ordinary bank access. Upstream the Summersville release moved twice in 24 hours: USGS 03189600 below the dam, stage only, fell from 9.66 feet at 4:45 a.m. Thursday to 8.15 by 7:45 a.m. and held 8.14 to 8.15 all day, then stepped back up Thursday night, 9.07 at 8:45 p.m., 10.16 at 9:45 and 11.07 at 10:45 p.m., and has held 11.06 to 11.08 since, 11.07 at 4:45 a.m.; the Gauley above Belva, USGS 03192000, ran 2,280 cfs at 5 a.m. Thursday, 1,600 by 10 a.m., 1,590 at noon, then drained through the afternoon, 1,050 at 5 p.m., 789 at 8, 719 at 11 p.m., and 697 cfs from 3 a.m. through 5 a.m. today, so Thursday night's step-up at the dam had not shown at Belva by 5 a.m. That is a reading of the traces, not a Corps statement, and it means the Kanawha's contribution to this pool was at its lowest of the week overnight, with more water on the way behind it. At 24.6 and flat the pool fishes structure, not slack: shad are the forage and skipjack are with them, so a white or pearl swimbait or a three-quarter-ounce spoon on the wing dams on the morning side, a blade bait or a three-inch paddletail on a half-ounce head along the riprap and the barge cuts, and a crawfish-pattern jig crawled down the riprap where it meets the mud for the smallmouth and the drum; with the pool a half foot lower than Thursday the upstream faces of the wing dams are shallower and the fish slide to the downstream eddy, and the lock wall at Byrd is the deep edge for the sauger and the hybrids on a jigging spoon or a live skipjack as the mornings cool.
waters.note: This is the pool side, 14 miles above R.C. Byrd Locks and Dam; USGS does not gauge the Byrd tailwater. The fetcher's 24.78 is the first point of its own two-day window, about 5:45 a.m. Wednesday, not 24 hours ago, and the trace pulled at 5:48 a.m., whose window opens at 6 a.m. Wednesday, reads 24.93 at its first point, so the two do not match today; the trace's true 24-hour change is down 0.51 feet from 25.16 at 5 a.m. Thursday, Thursday's edition reading, the window crest was 25.26 at 3 a.m. Thursday and the trough 24.54 Thursday evening, and the direction over the last hour is down 0.01, so the steady flag is wrong on the day and right at the hour. The fetcher's numbers and read string are printed as written; the Thursday trace and the overnight figures are the trace's, pulled at 5:48 a.m. No forecast is printed for this gauge. The Gauley figures are from USGS 03192000, above Belva, and the Summersville Dam figures from USGS 03189600, below the dam, which reports stage only, both pulled at 5:48 a.m. in the same request; the link between the dam, Belva and this pool is a reading of the traces, not anything the Corps said.

The trace runs 26.31 at 5 a.m. Thursday, the true 24-hour mark and Thursday's edition reading, 26.34 at 6, 26.36 at 7, 26.37 at 8, 26.34 at 9, 26.37 at 10, 26.19 at 11, 26.33 at noon, 26.28 at 1 p.m., 26.22 at 2, 26.20 at 3, 26.16 at 4, 26.07 at 5, 26.13 at 6, 26.14 at 7, 26.09 at 8, 26.08 at 9 and 10, 26.06 at 11 p.m., the window's overnight low, 26.09 at midnight and 1 a.m., 26.14 at 2, 26.10 at 3, 26.18 at 4 and 26.20 at 5 a.m. Against the 24-hour mark that is down 0.11, inside the band the fetcher called steady on Wednesday, and against the last hour it is up 0.02 and up 0.14 since 11 p.m.; the fetcher's 26.52 is the first point of its own two-day window, about 5:45 a.m. Wednesday (the trace's 6 a.m. Wednesday first point reads 26.49), and the 0.32 it flags as a fall is Wednesday's drainage, not Thursday's. No NWPS forecast was opened this morning; Thursday's edition carried the Weather Service's Wednesday-morning forecast of 26.3 by 2 a.m. today, and the gauge sat at 26.09 at that hour, a couple of tenths ahead of it. With the Summersville release cut further Thursday morning and then stepped back up Thursday night (see Point Pleasant), the Kanawha's contribution to this reach was at its lowest of the week overnight and will carry more again over the next day or two; that is a reading of the USGS traces. At 26.2 and flat the river below Byrd fishes the current edges off the structure: the forage is shad and skipjack with crawfish in the rock, so a white swimbait or a jigging spoon worked on the downstream face of the wing dams where the current folds, a half-ounce blade bait along the riprap for the sauger and the smallmouth, a crawfish-colored tube or jig on the riprap in the morning, and cut skipjack on the bottom in the barge cuts for the blues and the flatheads after dark; the lock wall fishes from the downstream side on a live skipjack for the hybrids when the lockages stir the water.
waters.note: This is the gauge below R.C. Byrd Locks and Dam, not the tailwater. The fetcher's 26.52 is the first point of its own two-day window, about 5:45 a.m. Wednesday, not 24 hours ago; the trace pulled at 5:48 a.m. opens at 6 a.m. Wednesday and reads 26.49 there, so the two are close but not identical today. The trace's true 24-hour change is down 0.11 feet from 26.31 at 5 a.m. Thursday, Thursday's edition reading, inside the band the fetcher called steady on Wednesday; the window's overnight low was 26.06 at 11 p.m. Thursday and the direction at 5 a.m. is up 0.02 on the hour and up 0.14 since 11 p.m., so the falling flag is wrong on the day and wrong at the hour. The Summersville cut and step-up and their link to this gauge are a reading of the USGS traces, not anything the Corps or the Weather Service said.

waters.read: Fish the moving water either side of high at 1:02 AM and 1:41 PM in the sound.
waters.working: Six days past the full moon and a day short of the last quarter, with the sound on the last of the night ebb at press time: the moon is 20.6 days old and 67% lit, the springs nearly run out and the neaps arriving with tomorrow's quarter, so the inlet runs about its average and softer than any morning this week. The U.S. Naval Observatory's phase table could not be read again this morning (its API refused the TLS handshake twice); the dates it gave Tuesday, the full moon Sept. 26, the last quarter Saturday, Oct. 3, at 13:25 Universal Time, 9:25 a.m. ET, and the new moon Oct. 10, are carried from Tuesday's edition and were not re-read today. The sound at Hampstead came off a 3.4-foot high at 1:02 a.m. and drains to a 0.5-foot low at 7:18 a.m., just after first light; it then fills to the day's big water, a 4.5-foot high at 1:41 p.m., a rise of 4.0 feet in about six and a half hours, and drains 3.6 feet to a 0.9-foot low at 8:31 p.m., well after dark, before the next flood runs through the night. Those are the four events; none spills past midnight tonight. The surf at Ocean City Beach pier runs ahead of the sound as it always does, and today its first event is Thursday's: high 11:42 p.m. Thursday at 4.0, low 5:37 a.m. at 0.4, high 12:26 p.m. at 5.5, low 6:59 p.m. at 0.8; today's lags from the two tables are 75 minutes on the midday high and 92 to 101 minutes on the lows, the long-ebb pattern the reference describes. For the crew's water two miles north of the inlet, that puts the tide stage first: the morning is the first of the flood from 7:18 a.m., the oyster bars and grass edges covering through late morning, the flats full and the drum pushed up into the grass and under the docks around the 1:41 p.m. high, then the ebb, and the last two hours of it, about 6:30 to 8:31 p.m., are the red drum window of the day, bait pulled out of the grass into the creek channels and the ICWW channel edges, the whole of it after sunset this time. Slack at 1:41 p.m. and 8:31 p.m. is dead water. The water at Beaufort, 60 miles up the coast, read 78.4 degrees at 5:36 a.m., up 1.4 from Thursday's 77.0 and still a summer number, which is what the shops are seeing too. What is running is a day old today, not a month: the Fisherman's Post Topsail and Sneads Ferry October report posted Thursday, Oct. 1, at 9 a.m. ET, and the feed carried it at 5:46 this morning. In it East Coast Sports has a run of slot red drum with some over-slots from the surf and piers, Spanish mackerel and bluefish plentiful from both, the pier anglers starting to see more king mackerel, the nearshore king bite still slow, red drum now the main target inshore and scattered all over the ICW, the creeks and the inlets, and no real word on speckled trout yet; Native Son has mullet all over the place and the red drum responding, docks producing and reds at creek mouths and grass lines, trout not ready yet beyond a few on topwater early, and glass minnows thick off the beach with excellent Spanish fishing; Spring Tide has reds still schooled in the bays, 22 to 28 inches and better the common size, topwater some days and cut bait others, and Spanish pushing inside the inlet on a high tide; Speckled Specialist has red drum good on Carolina-rigged live mullet, trout in the first hour of light on Heddon Spook Jrs. and then live shrimp under slip corks in 15 to 20 feet, and black drum of 3 to 4 pounds on shrimp at the bridges and oyster reefs; Carolina Flats has big mullet moving into the ICW and the bigger reds active on live finger mullet or Gulp under popping corks, with flounder as bycatch; Jolly Roger Pier has baitfish everywhere, multiple kings to 32 pounds, Spanish getting bigger, and night bottom fishing producing red drum to 31 inches, Virginia mullet, pompano, bluefish, black drum and some flounder; Surf City Pier has good-sized Spanish on Gotcha plugs, slot and occasional over-slot reds, and evening bottom fishing with black drum, mullet, spots and croakers; Seaview Pier has the mullet migration starting and a mixed bottom bag of flounder, sea mullet, spot, sheepshead, trout, black drum and the occasional red. Coastal Angler's Topsail column is still Sept. 1, 31 days old, and its Oct. 1 Sneads Ferry column is an offshore wahoo piece. Setups grounded in that and today's tide: on the morning flood, a Carolina-rigged live finger mullet, the bait the whole report is built on, along the grass edges and across the oyster bars as they cover, or a Gulp shrimp or a three-inch paddletail under a popping cork drifted along the edges, for the slot drum; first light, which lands on the bottom of the tide, a Spook Jr. or another walking topwater over the grass edges for the few trout that are showing, then live shrimp under a slip cork in the deeper holes; at the midday high, a weedless gold spoon or a soft plastic on a weighted swimbait hook in the flooded grass and under the docks for the drum; on the evening ebb, cut mullet or a live finger mullet on a Carolina rig fan-cast a couple of feet off the channel edges at the creek mouths for the drum in the dark, and a half-ounce bucktail with a Gulp trailer bounced through the channel edges for the flounder, which are release only and reported as bycatch; after dark, the dock lights on the night flood with a small white paddletail or a live shrimp under a float for the trout, and a fiddler crab or a piece of shrimp tight to the bridge pilings and oyster rocks on the moving water for the black drum and sheepshead. On the beach, Gotcha plugs and small metal or epoxy jigs for the Spanish on the flooding surf toward the 12:26 p.m. high, under the birds. The reference calendar lists October as the spot run's peak, with red drum, trout, bluefish, sea mullet and black drum, and the piers' spot and croaker lines fit it. Beach conditions: the Weather Service in Wilmington has a Dense Fog Advisory for Coastal Pender and the rest of its coast, issued 1:45 a.m. and running until 10 a.m., for visibility of a quarter mile or less; no rip current statement or Beach Hazards line is active.
